title: The Adaptive‐Innovative Ambidexterity Framework: A Qualitative Exploration of Ambidextrous Technology Use and Adaptive Outcomes
abstract: The COVID‐19 pandemic accelerated digitalisation across higher education (HE), compelling employees to adapt rapidly to online work environments. More specifically, it explains how crisis‐induced improvisations were either left as temporary workarounds or, through learning, transformed into sustained, digitally enabled work practices and microinnovations. This qualitative study examines how employees in Australian HE administration engage in adaptive ambidextrous technology‐use behaviours, balancing the exploitation of familiar tools and the exploration of new functionalities, underpinned by bricolage and adaptive performance. Using an interpretive qualitative approach, 38 semistructured interviews were thematically analysed with NVivo. The findings reveal that bricolage served as a catalyst for ambidextrous technology use, whereas adaptive performance behaviours and self‐directed and peer‐supported learning pathways mediated the sustainability of this use. These behaviours enhanced work‐related outcomes, including job satisfaction, productivity, error reduction, turnaround speed and task completion time. The study identifies innovative work practices as a novel outcome, where employees developed ‘microinnovations’ by reconfiguring workflows, automating tasks and integrating digital tools in new ways. This insight extends adaptive performance theory into the domain of creativity, bridging ambidexterity research with innovation management. The resulting adaptive‐innovative ambidexterity framework refines prior conceptualisations by situating bricolage as a catalyst, learning pathways as mediators and innovation as a distinct outcome. The study contributes theoretically by advancing microlevel understanding of adaptive ambidextrous technology use, and practically by highlighting how organisations can design digital strategies that foster both adaptation and innovation in postpandemic digital workplaces.
